assessment.rationale: This simulation is weak for the session-layer composition scenario because the pressure is about whether the transport-facing spec itself exposes a clean, sufficient boundary for the next layer. Moving explanatory promise meaning into a guide makes composition less self-contained and risks hiding binding details or conformance expectations outside the normative artifact.
strengths: Keeps protocol specs small and easier to implement mechanically.
May reduce clutter in the core normative document.
Plain-language guide prose could help onboarding when kept aligned.
weaknesses: Poor direct fit to a session-layer composition test.
Promise wording is displaced from the artifact that implementers must compose against.
Boundary clarity between transport spec and higher-layer expectations is weakened.
Failure modes from missing, stale, or divergent guide prose are not resolved.
risks: Normative meaning may drift between spec and guide.
Implementers may compose against underspecified session-layer expectations.
Long-term auditability suffers if guide prose changes or disappears.
open_questions: Can a minimal UDP-feed spec still state the exact payload promises needed by a session layer without relying on guide prose?
How are guide citations frozen or versioned so later auditors know which explanatory text shaped conformance?
What happens when implementers compose layers using only the normative spec and never read the guide?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
